common_name: Perkins Long Pod Okra (Classic Tall Southern Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Perkins Long Pod is a classic tall Southern heirloom okra and the parent line behind later spineless Perkins selections.

directions: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F. Perkins Long Pod is a traditional Southern heirloom okra grown for generations before the spineless Perkins strains were selected from it, producing heavy yields of long, ribbed, dark green pods on tall, vigorous plants that can reach 6 feet or more by season's end. Harvest pods every two to three days at 2-4 inches long for the most tender eating, since larger pods quickly turn woody and fibrous; regular picking keeps the plant producing continuously through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer. Stake or support plants in windy sites, and remove any overgrown pods promptly to keep new flowers and pods coming.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Okra Production

common_name: Jing Orange Okra (Chinese Heirloom Orange-Red Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra grown for its striking orange-red pods and stems, doubling as an ornamental as well as edible plant.

directions: Soak seed overnight before direct sowing an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra bearing vivid orange-red pods on stems and foliage tinged with the same warm color, making it as striking in the garden as it is productive, while retaining good tenderness a bit longer than typical green okra before pods toughen. Harvest at 2-4 inches for the best texture, picking every couple of days through the growing season to keep plants producing continuously in the Gulf South's long, hot summer. The colorful pods make an attractive addition to a mixed vegetable bed or ornamental edible border in addition to their culinary use in gumbo, frying, and pickling.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Okra Production

common_name: Bull Nose Pepper (Historic Jefferson-Era American Sweet Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented American sweet peppers, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello in the early 1800s.

directions: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented sweet pepper varieties in American gardens, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and preserved by seed savers as a living link to early American kitchen gardens, producing blocky, mild, thick-walled fruit that matures from green to red. It performs reliably through the long, hot Gulf South growing season on compact, productive plants well suited to garden beds or large containers. Harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage continued fruit set through summer.
sources: Monticello / Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

common_name: Mr. Big Pea (AAS-Winning Large-Podded Shelling Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner bred for unusually large, sweet pods on vigorous vines.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner prized for its unusually large, plump, sweet pods, often 4-5 inches long and packed with 9-10 large peas, produced heavily on vigorous vines over a fairly long harvest window for the cool season. Its exceptional pod size makes shelling faster and more rewarding than many standard shelling peas. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking every couple of days to encourage continued production before summer heat ends the crop.

common_name: Mascotte Bean (AAS-Winning Compact Container Filet Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil; Mascotte is a 2014 All-America Selections winner bred as a compact bush filet bean that holds its pods well above the foliage for easy picking, making it ideal for containers.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since the compact habit does not need the room a pole bean requires. Mascotte, a 2014 All-America Selections winner, was bred specifically for container growing, holding its slender, straight, tender filet-type pods well above the tidy, upright foliage where they are easy to spot and pick without stooping or digging through leaves. It matures quickly and produces a concentrated, heavy set of pods over a shorter window than many pole beans, making it well suited to succession planting in small beds or pots on a patio. Harvest pods young and slender for the best filet-bean texture, picking every day or two once production begins to keep new flowers coming.
